journal_name: Journal of Parallel and Distributed Computing

abstracts.abstract: The exponential growth of data-intensive computing workloads has exposed fundamental limitations in conventional parallel computing models that assume homogeneous processing elements and centralized coordination. This paper introduces a novel heterogeneous uncertainty-aware computation model (HUC) that fundamentally reconceptualizes how parallel algorithms handle variability in distributed environments. Unlike existing approaches that treat resource heterogeneity and communication uncertainty as secondary optimization concerns, HUC integrates these factors into the core computational model through probabilistic formalization of task completion times and data availability windows. We develop a comprehensive theoretical framework demonstrating that HUC enables the design of adaptive distributed algorithms with provable performance guarantees under bounded uncertainty. Our analysis establishes new complexity bounds for fundamental operations including load balancing, checkpoint placement, and fault-tolerant aggregations, proving that HUC achieves asymptotically optimal performance across varying uncertainty regimes. The model natively supports heterogeneous accelerator architectures including GPUs, FPGAs, and specialized ASICs within a unified scheduling framework. We prove that HUC enables a new class of resilient distributed algorithms that maintain sub-linear communication overhead even under adversarial node failures. This work establishes theoretical foundations for next-generation distributed systems that embrace rather than回避 uncertainty as a fundamental design constraint.

Scheduling theory for high-performance computing systems has traditionally relied on simplified task models that inadequately capture the communication-computation overlap characteristics of modern parallel architectures. This paper presents a rigorous theoretical analysis of a new task model incorporating multi-level memory hierarchies and overlapped communication phases, providing significantly tighter bounds on optimal makespan for distributed systems. We formulate the Hierarchical Communication-Aware Scheduling Problem (HCASP) and develop a polynomial-time approximation algorithm with a proven approximation ratio of 3/2 for arbitrary task graphs, improving upon the best known 2-approximation for classical models. For special classes including series-parallel and in-trees, we derive exact algorithms with pseudo-polynomial complexity. Our theoretical contributions include novel reduction techniques that transform HCASP instances to classical scheduling problems while preserving approximation guarantees. We extend the framework to heterogeneous computing environments and prove that our approach yields a 5/3-approximation for unrelated parallel machine scheduling with communication delays. Experimental validation on synthetic and real workload traces from production HPC systems confirms that the theoretical improvements translate to 15-25% makespan reductions compared to state-of-the-art heuristics. This work provides theoretically grounded foundations for developing practical scheduling algorithms that exploit communication-computation overlap in large-scale distributed systems.

This paper presents EdgeChain, a groundbreaking decentralized edge computing platform that fundamentally reimagines the relationship between edge devices, fog nodes, and cloud infrastructure. Unlike existing hierarchical edge architectures that maintain rigid central coordination, EdgeChain enables truly decentralized computation offloading through a novel Byzantine-fault-tolerant gossip protocol operating over volatile edge networks. The system introduces a programmable data plane abstraction allowing applications to specify fine-grained placement constraints while the runtime automatically handles consistency, replication, and failure recovery across heterogeneous edge resources. EdgeChain's architecture supports dynamic coalition formation among edge devices for collaborative processing, fundamentally shifting from the client-server paradigm to a cooperative peer ecosystem. We implement a complete system prototype integrating with Kubernetes through custom operators, enabling seamless deployment of distributed applications spanning cloud, fog, and edge tiers. Performance evaluation across 500+ geographically distributed edge nodes demonstrates that EdgeChain achieves sub-10ms response times for latency-sensitive workloads while maintaining strong consistency guarantees. The system's decentralized coordination overhead remains bounded by O(log n) messages per decision round, enabling scalability to thousands of participating edge devices. EdgeChain represents a paradigm shift toward resilient, privacy-preserving edge computing infrastructure suitable for next-generation Internet of Things deployments.

Big data platforms face increasing challenges in efficiently processing streaming workloads with diverse quality-of-service requirements within unified frameworks. This paper introduces StreamFusion, an enhanced data-intensive computing platform that significantly improves resource utilization and job completion times through novel cross-workload optimization techniques. StreamFusion addresses the fundamental tension between batch processing efficiency and stream processing latency by introducing adaptive execution modes that dynamically transition between processing paradigms based on workload characteristics. The system incorporates a novel cost-aware scheduler that jointly optimizes task placement, data partitioning, and pipeline composition across heterogeneous cluster resources. We implement StreamFusion as an extension to Apache Spark, maintaining API compatibility while fundamentally improving the runtime execution engine. Key innovations include predictive scaling mechanisms that anticipate workload bursts using historical patterns and reinforcement learning-based placement optimization that adapts to changing cluster conditions. Evaluation on Yahoo Streaming Benchmark and real production workloads demonstrates 40% latency reduction and 35% improvement in cluster resource utilization compared to vanilla Spark Streaming. The system scales linearly to 1000-node clusters with sub-second overhead for dynamic reconfiguration. StreamFusion provides production-ready infrastructure for organizations requiring high-throughput, low-latency stream processing with existing Spark-based big data ecosystems.
